mmaths-2019-individual-01.title: Find the error of the watch
mmaths-2019-individual-01.body:
Chicago is $5$ hours ahead of Hawaii, so the watch should have been moved $5$ hours forward, but it was moved $5$ hours back: it is now $10$ hours behind Chicago time. When the watch says $6{:}00$ the real Chicago time is $6{:}00+10$ hours, i.e. $4{:}00$ (in the night). He wants to wake up at $7{:}00$, so he should sleep $3$ more hours.

**Answer: 3 hours**

mmaths-2019-individual-02.title: Sectors around the hexagon
mmaths-2019-individual-02.body:
The interior angle of the hexagon is $120^\circ$, so near the tied vertex the leash can sweep the other $240^\circ$ with full length $20$: area $\frac{240}{360}\pi\cdot20^2=\frac{800\pi}{3}$.

On each side the leash can wrap around the neighbouring vertex: after going along one side (length $10$) the remaining $10$ of the leash swings through the exterior angle $60^\circ$ around that vertex: area $\frac{60}{360}\pi\cdot10^2=\frac{100\pi}{6}$, and there are two such sectors: $\frac{100\pi}{3}$. Wrapping further would need $10$ more along the next side, using up the whole leash ($10+10=20$), leaving length $0$.

Total: $\frac{800\pi}{3}+\frac{100\pi}{3}=300\pi$.

**Answer: $300\pi$**

mmaths-2019-individual-03.title: List outcomes by value
mmaths-2019-individual-03.body:
Ordered outcomes with sum $6$: permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$: $6$; permutations of $\{1,1,4\}$: $3$; and $(2,2,2)$: $1$. That is $10$ outcomes, all equally likely, and $6$ of them have distinct values. Probability $\frac6{10}=\frac35$.

**Answer: 3/5**

mmaths-2019-individual-04.title: Isosceles triangles at the center
mmaths-2019-individual-04.body:
Triangle $OBC$ is isosceles ($OB=OC$) with base angles $36^\circ$, so $\angle BOC=180^\circ-72^\circ=108^\circ$.

*$C$ on the minor arc $AB$:* then $\angle AOC=110^\circ-108^\circ=2^\circ$ and, since $OA=OC$, $\angle CAO=\frac{180^\circ-2^\circ}2=89^\circ$.

*$C$ on the other side:* $\angle AOC=360^\circ-110^\circ-108^\circ=142^\circ$ and $\angle CAO=\frac{180^\circ-142^\circ}{2}=19^\circ$.

The difference is $89^\circ-19^\circ=70^\circ$.

**Answer: 70**

mmaths-2019-individual-05.title: Expected difference of the last two piles
mmaths-2019-individual-05.body:
Let the piles have weights $w_1,\dots,w_4$ (a permutation of $1,2,3,4$). Say pile $i$ is distributed first, then pile $l$, and the piles $j,k$ remain. After the first step the remaining piles weigh $w_m+\frac{w_i}{3}$. When pile $l$ is distributed, $j$ and $k$ each receive half of $w_l+\frac{w_i}3$. Final weights: $w_j+\frac{w_i}{3}+\frac{w_l}{2}+\frac{w_i}{6}=w_j+\frac{w_i+w_l}{2}$ and similarly $w_k+\frac{w_i+w_l}2$. So the two final piles differ by exactly $|w_j-w_k|$, and they weigh $10$ in total. The surviving pair $\{j,k\}$ is a uniformly random pair of the original piles, whose weight differences are $1,2,3,1,2,1$ with average $\frac{10}{6}=\frac53$.

The larger final pile weighs $\frac{10+|w_j-w_k|}{2}$, with expectation $5+\frac12\cdot\frac53=\frac{35}6$.

**Answer: 35/6**

mmaths-2019-individual-06.title: Divisibility rules in base 8
mmaths-2019-individual-06.body:
*Digit $c$:* $15!$ has $\lfloor15/2\rfloor+\lfloor15/4\rfloor+\lfloor15/8\rfloor=7+3+1=11$ factors of $2$, so $2^{11}$ divides it; $8^3=2^9$ divides $15!$ and the last three base-$8$ digits are $0$: $c=0$.

*Digits $a,b$:* Since $8\equiv1\pmod7$, a number is divisible by $7$ iff its base-$8$ digit sum is. $15!$ is divisible by $7$: $2+3+0+1+6+7+3+5+6+a+b=33+a+b\equiv0\pmod7$, so $a+b\equiv2\pmod 7$, i.e. $a+b\in\{2,9,16\}$. Since $8\equiv-1\pmod9$, divisibility by $9$ is equivalent to the alternating digit sum being a multiple of $9$: $2-3+0-1+6-7+3-5+6-a+b-0+0-0=1-a+b\equiv0\pmod9$, so $b-a=-1$ (as $|b-a|\le7$). Then $a+b=2a-1$ is odd, so it equals $9$: $a=5$, $b=4$.

So $\overline{abc}=540$.

**Answer: 540**

mmaths-2019-individual-07.title: Area ratios along lines

mmaths-2019-individual-08.title: Power mean
mmaths-2019-individual-08.body:
By the power mean inequality, $\frac{|x|+|y|+|z|}{3}\le\left(\frac{x^4+y^4+z^4}{3}\right)^{1/4}=3^{-1/4}$, so $|x+y+z|\le3^{3/4}$, with equality when $x=y=z=\pm3^{-1/4}$. Hence $a=3^{3/4}$ and $b=-3^{3/4}$. The same bound applies to $x-y-z=x+(-y)+(-z)$ (the constraint is unchanged by the sign flips): $c=3^{3/4}$, $d=-3^{3/4}$. Then $abcd=(3^{3/4})^4=3^3=27$.

**Answer: 27**

mmaths-2019-individual-09.title: Split odds and evens
mmaths-2019-individual-09.body:
Elements differing by $2$ have the same parity, so odds $\{1,3,5,7,9,11\}$ and evens $\{2,4,6,8,10\}$ can be treated separately. Within each group the forbidden pairs are neighbours, so we count subsets of a path with no two consecutive elements. Let $a_n$ be that number for $n$ elements: $a_0=1$, $a_1=2$, $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ (either the last element is out, or it is in and the previous one is out). So $a_2=3,a_3=5,a_4=8,a_5=13,a_6=21$. There are $6$ odds and $5$ evens: $a_6a_5=21\cdot13=273$.

**Answer: 273**

mmaths-2019-individual-10.title: Integer square condition
mmaths-2019-individual-10.body:
$x^2+y^2=72+2y^2$, so we want $y^2$ as large as possible. $(x+y)^2=x^2+y^2+2xy=72+2y^2+2\sqrt{y^2(y^2+72)}$. For this to be an integer, $\sqrt{y^4+72y^2}$ must be rational, hence an integer $m$ (with $y^2$ an integer). Then $(y^2+36)^2-m^2=36^2=1296$, so $(y^2+36-m)(y^2+36+m)=1296$ with both factors positive of the same parity, hence even. The sum of the factors is $2(y^2+36)$, which is largest for the most unbalanced pair $2\cdot648$: $y^2+36=325$, $y^2=289$, $m=323$. Then $y=17$, $x^2=361$, $x=19$, $(x+y)^2=1296$, and $x^2+y^2=650$.

**Answer: 650**

mmaths-2019-individual-11.title: Count by building from an ear
mmaths-2019-individual-11.body:
Every triangulation of the $2019$-gon has $2017$ triangles. Each triangle has at least one polygon side, and there are $2019$ polygon sides, so exactly two triangles have two polygon sides (the ears) and $2015$ have exactly one; the triangles form a path. Build it from one ear: choose the ear ($2019$ ways, three consecutive vertices). It has one interior side; the next triangle on this side has exactly $2$ choices (its third vertex is the next vertex on either side), and so on for $2015$ steps, the last triangle being forced. That gives $2019\cdot2^{2015}$, but each triangulation is counted twice (starting from either ear), so $N=2019\cdot2^{2014}$. As $2019$ is odd, the largest $a$ is $2014$.

**Answer: 2014**

mmaths-2019-individual-12.title: Bipartite 2-regular graphs
mmaths-2019-individual-12.body:
A valid arrangement is a simple bipartite graph on $5$ rows and $5$ columns in which every vertex has degree $2$, i.e. a disjoint union of even cycles, each cycle using $k\ge2$ rows and $k$ columns. With $5$ rows the possible cycle structures are one cycle with $k=5$, or two cycles with $k=2$ and $k=3$.

- *One cycle ($k=5$):* the number of Hamiltonian cycles in $K_{5,5}$ is $\frac{5!\,4!}{2}=1440$.
- *Cycles with $k=2$ and $k=3$:* choose the $2$ rows and $2$ columns of the short cycle ($\binom52^2=100$ ways); $K_{2,2}$ has $1$ Hamiltonian cycle and $K_{3,3}$ has $\frac{3!\,2!}{2}=6$: $100\cdot6=600$.

Total $1440+600=2040$.

**Answer: 2040**
